Discover
dis-KUV-er
verb
From Old French descovrir, “to uncover, unroof, lay bare,” from Latin dis- (undo) and cooperire, “to cover.” To discover is literally to dis-cover — to take the covering off. The modern sense of finding out for the first time is a later narrowing.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV to discover is to uncover, to strip bare, to lay open what was hidden — not, as with us, to be the first to find a thing out. The word still wears its parts on its face: to dis-cover is to take the cover off. When Jonathan and his armour-bearer resolve to “discover ourselves unto them” (1Sa 14:8), they do not intend to explore the Philistines; they mean to reveal themselves, to step out of hiding into the enemy’s sight. When Solomon warns, “discover not a secret to another” (Pro 25:9), he forbids the uncovering of a confidence — the laying bare of what should stay hid. The word rises to grandeur in the poets. The voice of the LORD “discovereth the forests” (Psa 29:9): the thunder-storm of God strips the woods naked, tearing the leaves away till the bare trunks stand exposed. And Habakkuk sees the LORD go out for the salvation of His people, “discovering the foundation unto the neck” (Hab 3:13) — laying the enemy open from top to bottom, uncovering him to utter ruin. So the word is a word of exposure. It suits the God before whom all things are naked and opened; He is the great Discoverer, not because He learns what He did not know, but because He strips the covering from every hidden thing and brings the secrets of the heart to light. Let the sinner remember it, and the saint take comfort: nothing stays covered before Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

To uncover, reveal, lay bare — to take the covering off, not to find out anew.

DISCOVER, to uncover; to lay open to view; to disclose; to reveal.

From Old French descovrir, from Latin dis- and cooperire, “to cover.”

The literal sense is to un-cover; the sense of finding out first is a later narrowing.

Jonathan would discover himself — reveal himself — to the Philistines (1Sa 14:8).

The voice of the LORD discovereth (strips bare) the forests (Psa 29:9).

Key Scripture

1Sa 14:8 — "Then said Jonathan, Behold, we will pass over unto these men, and we will discover ourselves unto them."

Pro 25:9 — "Debate thy cause with thy neighbour himself; and discover not a secret to another:"

Psa 29:9 — "The voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve, and discovereth the forests: and in his temple doth every one speak of his glory."

Hab 3:13 — "Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah."

Modern Corruption

A word that once meant to uncover now means to find out — exposure narrowed into information.

expand to see more

The drift is honest and complete: for us, to discover is to learn something for the first time, the explorer’s or the scientist’s word. For the AV it is to uncover, the same act as stripping a roof or lifting a veil. The modern reader who meets Jonathan “discovering” himself imagines him detecting or spying out the Philistines, when he means to show himself openly to them. Restore the old sense and the poetry stands upright: God’s thunder does not investigate the forests but strips them bare, and His arm does not find out the wicked but lays him open to the neck.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the terrible openness of all things before God. To discover, in the old tongue, is what the Last Day will do to every man: there is nothing covered that shall not be revealed. The Judge does not discover in our sense, learning our sins as news; He discovers in the old sense, uncovering what was always seen, stripping the fig-leaves from the conscience and setting the hidden things in the light of His face. For the impenitent this is dread; for the pardoned it is peace, for the covering that God has torn from their sin He has replaced with the righteousness of Christ, and under that covering they shall stand discovered and unashamed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means to uncover and lay bare, keeping its parts — dis-cover.

expand to see more

Discover — from Old French descovrir, “to uncover.”

Literally dis- (undo) + cover: to take the covering off.

In the KJV it means to reveal, expose, lay bare — never to find out anew.

“Discover not a secret” (Pro 25:9): do not uncover a confidence.

God discovers the forests and the foundations — strips them naked (Psa 29:9; Hab 3:13).

Usage

"To discover a secret in the KJV is to betray it, not to learn it."

"Jonathan discovered himself — stepped from hiding into the enemy’s sight."

"The thunder of God discovereth the forests, stripping them bare."
